bib.title: Introduction to Machine Learning with Python, Chapter 1: Introduction

question: What is machine learning, what problems does it solve, and how does one build and evaluate a first supervised model with scikit-learn?
contributions: Defines supervised vs unsupervised learning, samples, features, labels and classes
Walks through a first model: k-NN on Iris with a train/test split and accuracy
Introduces the Python stack (NumPy, SciPy, pandas, matplotlib, Jupyter, scikit-learn)

limits: Single random split, one seed, k=1; no confidence interval, cross-validation or tuning (deferred to later chapters).
'Under some mathematical assumptions' about generalisation is never spelled out.

Dated: Python 3.5.2, scikit-learn 0.18, pandas 0.18.1, NumPy 1.11.1; pd.scatter_matrix is now pandas.plotting.scatter_matrix; Python 2 compatibility advice, Enthought Canopy, Python(x,y), %matplotlib notebook and sklearn.cross_validation-era notes are obsolete; KNeighborsClassifier repr (n_jobs=1) differs in current versions.
Does not mention stratified splitting, data leakage in preprocessing, or class-imbalance accuracy pitfalls.
practices: Never evaluate on the data used to build the model, because the model can memorise it; hold out a test set (p.17).
Shuffle before splitting, since Iris is sorted by label and a last-25% test set would hold only class 2 (p.18).
Fix random_state for every randomised procedure so results are reproducible (p.18).
Look at your data first (pair plot) to check the task is solvable and to find unit inconsistencies (p.19-20).
Understand the task and data before choosing an algorithm; ask what question, what features, how success is measured, how it fits the product (pp.4-5).
Use sparse matrices for mostly-zero data and build them directly in COO/CSR when dense will not fit in memory (p.9).
Data shape convention: X is 2D (samples x features), y is 1D; predict needs a 2D array even for one sample (p.17,22).
